hint: An ancient civilization marked the start of a long count
funFact: Did you know? The Maya Long Count's famous 2012 end wasn't an apocalypse — it was just their calendar rolling over like a car odometer hitting 100,000.

hint: The Prophet's passing transformed a civilization
funFact: Did you know? Muhammad's tomb in Medina is draped in green — and pilgrims still leave letters addressed to him, 1,400 years on.

hint: From York, a future emperor was proclaimed by his legions
funFact: Did you know? Constantine was proclaimed emperor in York, England — the only Roman emperor 'made' on British soil.

hint: Flames engulfed the Eternal City for six days
funFact: Did you know? Nero probably didn't fiddle while Rome burned — fiddles didn't exist yet. He was 50km away in Antium, allegedly writing poetry.

hint: A legendary conqueror fell ill and died in Babylon
funFact: Did you know? Alexander the Great's body reportedly stayed uncorrupted for six days in the Babylon heat. Modern scholars think he may not have been fully dead yet.

hint: A Persian king entered Babylon without a battle
funFact: Did you know? Cyrus the Great let the conquered Babylonians keep their gods and temples — his Cyrus Cylinder is sometimes called the first human rights charter.

hint: Three hundred Spartans held the pass against a million
funFact: Did you know? The 300 Spartans at Thermopylae actually had around 7,000 Greek allies with them. Hollywood just prefers round numbers.

hint: Greek triremes trapped and crushed a Persian fleet
funFact: Did you know? At Salamis, Persian ships outnumbered Greek ones 3-to-1 — but the narrow strait meant half the Persian fleet couldn't even reach the fight.

hint: A reformed calendar finally aligned with the sun
funFact: Did you know? Caesar's Julian calendar was so off it drifted by 11 minutes a year — small, but enough to need a 10-day skip 1,600 years later.

hint: Barbarian Goths breached the walls of the Eternal City
event: Sack of Rome by the Visigoths
funFact: Did you know? The 'Sack of Rome' lasted only three days and the Visigoths reportedly spared churches — a surprisingly polite apocalypse.

hint: An arrow (perhaps) and a crown changed English history
funFact: Did you know? The Bayeux Tapestry depicting Hastings is 70 metres long and still missing its final panel — nobody knows how it originally ended.

hint: A pope's speech launched centuries of holy wars
event: Pope Urban II calls the First Crusade
funFact: Did you know? Pope Urban II promised crusaders instant forgiveness for all their sins. The recruitment offer basically wrote itself.

hint: Crusaders breached walls and claimed a holy city
funFact: Did you know? When crusaders took Jerusalem, survivors described blood 'up to the horses' bridles' — almost certainly an exaggeration, but the chroniclers were keen.

hint: The last Roman empire fell when cannons broke ancient walls
funFact: Did you know? Constantinople fell partly because a small side gate, the Kerkoporta, was left unlocked. One door, one empire.

hint: A peasant girl born who would hear voices and save France
funFact: Did you know? Joan of Arc started hearing saints at 13. By 17 she was leading armies. By 19 she was dead. History rarely moves that fast.

hint: A teenage warrior-saint burned at the stake in Rouen
funFact: Did you know? Joan's executioners burned her three times to ensure nothing remained — they'd heard rumours people might collect relics.

hint: Scottish spearmen routed English knights in a bog
funFact: Did you know? Robert the Bruce won Bannockburn partly thanks to caltrops and concealed pits — medieval land mines made of iron spikes.

hint: English longbows devastated French knights in the mud
funFact: Did you know? At Agincourt, English longbowmen shot so many arrows so fast that French knights died face-down in mud, crushed by their own retreating side.

hint: A renaissance poet's pen transformed Italian literature
funFact: Did you know? Dante invented the word 'quintessence' in the Divine Comedy — the fifth element beyond earth, water, air, and fire.

hint: A plague arrived by ship and would claim half of Europe
funFact: Did you know? Black Death–era Londoners tried everything — prayer, bloodletting, cat massacres. Killing cats only helped the rats, and the rats carried the fleas.

hint: A Portuguese fleet sailed west and stumbled upon Brazil
funFact: Did you know? Cabral was supposedly sailing to India when he 'accidentally' bumped into Brazil. Historians still argue whether it was really an accident.

hint: Five ships set sail to circumnavigate the entire globe
funFact: Did you know? Magellan named the Pacific 'pacific' because it was calm when he crossed it. Anyone who's flown across it in a storm knows he got lucky.

hint: One battered ship completed the first trip around the world
funFact: Did you know? Only 18 of Magellan's 270 crew made it home. Magellan himself died in the Philippines, two-thirds of the way around.

hint: A Spanish conquistador entered the Aztec capital in awe
funFact: Did you know? Cortés had just 600 men when he entered Tenochtitlán — a city bigger than any in Spain. Montezuma reportedly welcomed him with flowers.

hint: A conquistador captured an Inca emperor with treachery
funFact: Did you know? Pizarro conquered an empire of 6 million with 168 men. He'd been a pig herder before turning conquistador.

hint: A papal decree reformed the calendar, skipping ten days
funFact: Did you know? When the Gregorian calendar skipped 10 days in 1582, some towns rioted — people genuinely thought their lives had been shortened.

hint: A bard of Avon was born who would define English theatre
funFact: Did you know? We don't actually know Shakespeare's birthday — only his baptism date. April 23 is a best guess, conveniently also the day he died.

hint: The Bard's quill fell silent in Stratford-upon-Avon
funFact: Did you know? Shakespeare's grave curses anyone who moves his bones: 'Blessed be the man that spares these stones, / And cursed be he that moves my bones.'

hint: The father of modern astronomy breathed his last in Italy
funFact: Did you know? Galileo was still under house arrest when he died. The Vatican only formally admitted he'd been right about the Earth in 1992.

hint: A Powhatan woman wed an Englishman, bridging two worlds
event: Marriage of Pocahontas and John Rolfe
funFact: Did you know? Pocahontas was about 17 when she married John Rolfe — and renamed 'Rebecca'. She died in England aged roughly 21.

hint: A baker's oven sparked an inferno that remade a capital
funFact: Did you know? The Great Fire of London officially killed only six people — though the actual toll was almost certainly much higher, just unrecorded among the poor.

hint: A Quaker received a vast charter for a wooded colony
funFact: Did you know? Pennsylvania means 'Penn's Woods' — but it's named after William Penn's father, not William himself. He found it mildly embarrassing.

hint: Parliament declared rights above the power of a king
funFact: Did you know? The English Bill of Rights is the direct ancestor of the US Bill of Rights — and it's still in force today, over 330 years later.

hint: A Dutch prince sailed to England and a king fled
funFact: Did you know? The 'Glorious Revolution' was basically an invited invasion — English nobles literally wrote to William of Orange asking him to come take over.

hint: Two kingdoms merged into one united island nation
funFact: Did you know? Scotland joined the union partly because it went bankrupt trying to colonise Panama. The Darien scheme lost about a quarter of the country's wealth.

hint: Ten amendments enshrined the people's fundamental rights
funFact: Did you know? The original Bill of Rights had 12 amendments — only 10 passed. One of the unpassed ones finally made it in 1992, after 203 years.

hint: A king lost his head to the guillotine in a Paris square
funFact: Did you know? Louis XVI's last words were reportedly 'I die innocent' — but the drum roll drowned him out. Royal dignity versus stage management.

hint: A queen followed her husband to the guillotine
funFact: Did you know? Marie Antoinette apologised to her executioner for stepping on his foot. Nine months pregnant at her marriage, guillotined at 37.

hint: The shot heard round the world echoed at a village green
funFact: Did you know? Paul Revere didn't shout 'The British are coming!' — most colonists still considered themselves British. He likely said 'The Regulars are coming out.'

hint: A British general surrendered, sealing American independence
funFact: Did you know? When the British surrendered at Yorktown, their band reportedly played 'The World Turned Upside Down' — a song about everything going wrong.

hint: A Caribbean island became the first free black republic
funFact: Did you know? Haiti was the first country founded by formerly enslaved people — and the only successful slave revolution in history.

hint: A general crowned himself emperor in Notre-Dame
funFact: Did you know? Napoleon crowned himself — literally took the crown from the Pope's hands. Nothing says 'self-made man' like bypassing divine authority.

hint: A one-armed admiral won a decisive sea battle and died
funFact: Did you know? Nelson won Trafalgar but was shot by a French sniper. He died below deck, reportedly asking to be kissed goodbye by Captain Hardy.

hint: A grand army crossed a river heading east to disaster
funFact: Did you know? Napoleon invaded Russia with 600,000 men. About 30,000 came back. The Russian winter wasn't kind to French fashion.

hint: Rockets and bombs inspired a national anthem at a fort
funFact: Did you know? Francis Scott Key wrote the Star-Spangled Banner as a poem. The tune he borrowed was a British drinking song — notoriously hard to sing.

hint: A second war between America and Britain officially began
funFact: Did you know? The War of 1812 actually ended in a draw — but the Battle of New Orleans was fought two weeks AFTER the peace treaty was signed. Slow mail.

hint: An American president confirmed gold had been found out west
funFact: Did you know? The 1848 California Gold Rush caused such a labour shortage that San Francisco harbour filled with 500 abandoned ships — crews ran off to mine gold.

hint: A young naturalist set sail on a voyage that would reshape biology
funFact: Did you know? Darwin was originally going to be an Anglican priest. The Beagle was meant to be a five-year gap year. He was seasick the entire voyage.

hint: A revolutionary book argued species change over time
event: Publication of On the Origin of Species
funFact: Did you know? Origin of Species sold out its first print run on day one — 1,250 copies. Darwin waited 20 years to publish, terrified of the backlash.

hint: A canal connected two seas and reshaped global trade
funFact: Did you know? The Suez Canal took 10 years and over 100,000 workers to dig — many with shovels, by hand. It's still the world's busiest shipping shortcut.

hint: The first words transmitted by wire: come here, I want you
event: Alexander Graham Bell's first phone call
funFact: Did you know? Bell's first words on the phone — 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you' — may have been called because he'd just spilled acid on himself.

hint: A first dictionary defined a young nation's language
funFact: Did you know? Webster's Dictionary was the reason Americans spell 'color' without the 'u'. Noah Webster wanted a distinctly American English.

hint: A copper lady was unveiled in a New York harbour
event: Dedication of the Statue of Liberty
funFact: Did you know? The Statue of Liberty arrived in 214 crates — and nearly didn't get built because America couldn't afford the pedestal. A newspaper fundraiser saved it.

hint: An iron tower opened for a fair and became a symbol of a city
funFact: Did you know? Parisians hated the Eiffel Tower at first — writers called it a 'truly tragic street lamp'. It was only supposed to stand for 20 years.

hint: A massive fair showcased a white city on a lakefront
funFact: Did you know? The Chicago World's Fair introduced the Ferris wheel, Juicy Fruit, and spray paint. It also inspired the Emerald City in The Wizard of Oz.

hint: A society was founded to explore and map the world
funFact: Did you know? National Geographic's iconic yellow border wasn't chosen for any symbolic reason — editors just picked yellow because it stood out on magazine racks.

hint: The first license plates for motorised vehicles appeared
event: First automobile license plates issued in Paris
funFact: Did you know? Paris introduced number plates because early cars kept running over pedestrians and speeding off. 'Hit and run' is older than most think.

hint: Shadows moved on a screen in a Parisian café
event: First public film screening by Lumière brothers
funFact: Did you know? The Lumières' first public film showed workers leaving a factory. Audiences reportedly ducked when a train appeared to rush at them.

hint: A patent was filed for a horseless carriage in Germany
funFact: Did you know? Selden's patent was later overturned — partly thanks to Henry Ford, who refused to pay royalties and fought through the courts for 8 years.

hint: A Swedish inventor's will established prizes for peace and science
funFact: Did you know? Nobel founded his prizes because a French newspaper accidentally published his obituary early — calling him 'the merchant of death'. He didn't want to be remembered that way.

hint: An empress of an era passed, ending 63 years of reign
funFact: Did you know? Victoria reigned 63 years — longer than any British monarch except Elizabeth II. At her death, her great-grandchildren sat on most of Europe's thrones.

hint: Gold was found in a Yukon creek, sparking a northern rush
funFact: Did you know? Gold miners from the Klondike rush included a young author named Jack London. He found no gold but plenty of material for books.

hint: Guglielmo Marconi received the letter 'S' sent across the ocean in Morse code.
funFact: Did you know? Marconi's first transatlantic signal was just the letter 'S' in Morse code — three dots. Critics insisted it was impossible, then quietly went quiet.

hint: A British explorer reached the pole, only to find he was second
funFact: Did you know? Scott reached the South Pole only to find Amundsen's Norwegian flag already there, left 34 days earlier. He wrote 'Great God! this is an awful place.'

hint: Mobilisation orders plunged Europe into total war
event: Germany declares war on Russia (WWI begins)
funFact: Did you know? WWI's spark wasn't the assassination alone — it was that Austria's 10-point ultimatum was designed to be impossible to accept.

hint: A torpedo sank a luxury liner, turning opinion against Germany
funFact: Did you know? The Lusitania was carrying 173 tonnes of ammunition when it was torpedoed — something the British denied for almost a century.

hint: The bloodiest day in British military history on the Somme
event: First day of the Battle of the Somme
funFact: Did you know? On day one of the Somme, 57,470 British soldiers were killed, wounded, or missing. It remains the bloodiest day in British military history.

hint: Bolsheviks seized power in a revolution that reshaped the world
funFact: Did you know? Lenin arrived in Russia via a 'sealed train' from Switzerland. Germany hoped he'd destabilise Russia. It worked — spectacularly.

hint: An emperor's voice on radio announced unconditional surrender
funFact: Did you know? Japan surrendered before anyone knew WHY — the Emperor's broadcast used such formal language, most citizens couldn't understand him.

hint: The US Senate rejected a league meant to prevent future wars
event: US Senate rejects League of Nations
funFact: Did you know? The US Senate rejected the League of Nations partly because Wilson refused to compromise. America wasn't in the league it had invented.

hint: A radio station broadcast election results for the first time
funFact: Did you know? KDKA's first broadcast was the 1920 election results — before most listeners even had news radios. Families huddled around crystal sets.

hint: British workers walked out in solidarity, paralysing the nation
funFact: Did you know? During the British General Strike, Oxbridge students volunteered to drive buses and trains. Several crashed them. Solidarity, sort of.

hint: A solo pilot touched down in Paris after 33 hours over the Atlantic
funFact: Did you know? Lindbergh's 33-hour flight ran on one sandwich. He stayed awake by flying inches above the waves to feel the spray on his face.

hint: A jazz singer's voice was heard from the silver screen
event: The Jazz Singer (first talkie film) premieres
funFact: Did you know? The Jazz Singer had just two minutes of synchronised dialogue. Its famous line — 'You ain't heard nothin' yet!' — was improvised.

hint: A cartoon mouse debuted with synchronised sound
funFact: Did you know? Mickey Mouse was originally going to be called Mortimer. Walt Disney's wife reportedly said 'Mortimer sounds pompous' — so Mickey it was.

hint: The market crashed on a black Tuesday, triggering depression
funFact: Did you know? Some Wall Street messengers on Black Tuesday were so overwhelmed they just threw share certificates in the street. Pedestrians picked them up as souvenirs.

hint: A mouldy petri dish led to a lifesaving discovery
funFact: Did you know? Fleming discovered penicillin because he was messy — he went on holiday and left a Petri dish uncovered. History's most productive cleaning fail.

hint: A chancellor was appointed who would plunge the world into darkness
funFact: Did you know? Hitler became Chancellor through legal appointment, not a coup. The people who put him there thought they could control him. They could not.

hint: A parliament building was set ablaze, enabling emergency powers
funFact: Did you know? The Reichstag fire conveniently happened just before elections. Historians still argue whether the Nazis set it themselves — but they sure benefited.

hint: A new president told a nation the only thing to fear is fear itself
funFact: Did you know? FDR's New Deal created the Civilian Conservation Corps, which planted over 3 BILLION trees. Many US forests today started as stimulus projects.

hint: The night of broken glass shattered Jewish shops across Germany
funFact: Did you know? 'Kristallnacht' means 'Crystal Night' — named for the glass from thousands of shattered Jewish shop windows. The Nazis then billed the victims for the cleanup.

hint: A promise of 'peace for our time' that would prove hollow
funFact: Did you know? Chamberlain famously waved the Munich Agreement declaring 'peace for our time'. War broke out 11 months later.

hint: Britain and France declared war, beginning a second world war
event: Britain and France declare war on Germany
funFact: Did you know? Britain declared war on Germany at 11am on a Sunday. Three minutes later, an air raid siren went off in London — a false alarm. Everyone's nerves were already shot.

hint: An armada of small boats rescued soldiers from a beach
funFact: Did you know? 'Little ships' of Dunkirk included fishing boats, paddle steamers, even pleasure yachts. One was crewed by two teenagers. They rescued 338,000 men.

hint: Luftwaffe bombers sought to break British spirit from above
funFact: Did you know? RAF pilots during the Battle of Britain had an average combat life of 4 weeks. Churchill called them 'the Few' for a reason.

hint: A massive surprise invasion shattered a non-aggression pact
funFact: Did you know? Operation Barbarossa was the largest invasion in history — 3 million troops. Hitler launched it on the same date as Napoleon's disastrous 1812 invasion. Why did he think this would go differently?

hint: A frozen siege ended with German surrender on the Volga
funFact: Did you know? Stalingrad lasted 200 days and killed around 2 million. The Soviet 62nd Army fought so fiercely that Germans started calling it 'Rattenkrieg' — rat war.

hint: Soviet and American soldiers shook hands at a German river
event: Allied forces meet at the Elbe River
funFact: Did you know? At the Elbe, American and Soviet soldiers swapped cigarettes, watches, and vodka. The next few years of politics went somewhat less warmly.

hint: A dictator took his own life in a Berlin bunker
funFact: Did you know? Hitler married Eva Braun about 40 hours before they both died. Their bodies were doused in petrol and burned in the Reich Chancellery garden.

hint: A second atomic flash devastated a port city in Japan
funFact: Did you know? The Nagasaki bomb 'Fat Man' wasn't even the first target — clouds obscured Kokura. Nagasaki was the backup city. Weather decided the death of 80,000 people.

hint: A new international body was established to maintain peace
funFact: Did you know? The UN's first session was held in London in January 1946 — in Methodist Central Hall, Westminster. The building is still there today.

hint: A midnight chime marked the birth of two nations from one
funFact: Did you know? Indian independence came at midnight — a time chosen by astrologers as auspicious. Nehru delivered his 'tryst with destiny' speech minutes earlier.

hint: Troops crossed a parallel, starting a cold war's hot conflict
funFact: Did you know? The Korean War was technically never ended — 1953 was only an armistice. North and South Korea are still formally at war, 70+ years later.

hint: An armistice froze a conflict that has never officially ended
funFact: Did you know? The Korean armistice was negotiated at Panmunjom, where diplomats from both sides refused to eat together. They used separate tables — for two years.

hint: A young princess became queen while in Kenya
funFact: Did you know? Elizabeth II learned she was Queen while up a tree — literally. She was watching wildlife in Kenya when her father died back in England.

hint: A four-minute barrier in athletics was finally shattered
event: Roger Bannister runs a sub-4-minute mile
funFact: Did you know? Doctors genuinely believed a sub-4-minute mile was physically impossible. Once Bannister broke it, 37 people did the same within the next year.

hint: A refusal to give up a bus seat sparked a movement
event: Rosa Parks refuses to give up her seat
funFact: Did you know? Rosa Parks wasn't just tired — she was a trained activist, secretary of the local NAACP. The 'weary seamstress' framing undersells her courage.

hint: A bus boycott began that would last over a year
funFact: Did you know? The Montgomery bus boycott lasted 381 days. Many protesters walked over 10 miles a day. Some used carpools run partly by the churches.

hint: An invasion over a canal brought Cold War tensions to boiling
funFact: Did you know? The Suez Crisis ended when the US — furious at being kept in the dark — threatened to tank the British pound. Britain caved in days.

hint: A dog named Laika became the first animal to orbit Earth
funFact: Did you know? Laika the dog was the first living creature in orbit — but she died within hours from overheating. The USSR only admitted this in 2002.

hint: Four students sat down at a lunch counter and refused to leave
funFact: Did you know? The Greensboro sit-ins were sparked by four college students ordering coffee. Within two months, 50 cities had sit-ins. Teenagers with caffeine: a force.

hint: A failed invasion at a bay embarrassed a superpower
funFact: Did you know? The Bay of Pigs invasion failed so badly that Kennedy reportedly said: 'How could I have been so stupid?' The CIA had assured him it would work.

hint: A wall went up overnight, dividing a city for 28 years
event: Construction of the Berlin Wall begins
funFact: Did you know? The Berlin Wall went up literally overnight — East German troops rolled out barbed wire while Berliners slept. By morning, families were split.

hint: Television showed missile sites that brought the world to the brink
funFact: Did you know? During the Cuban Missile Crisis, the world came closer to nuclear war than most people realised. A Soviet sub captain had orders to launch — and was talked out of it by his second officer.

hint: A tense standoff ended when Soviet ships turned back
funFact: Did you know? Khrushchev later said the Cuban Missile Crisis made him feel like 'sitting on a volcano'. Both leaders quietly took down missile sites in their own countries afterwards.

hint: A cosmonaut became the first woman to orbit the Earth
funFact: Did you know? Tereshkova, first woman in space, was a textile worker and amateur skydiver before becoming a cosmonaut. She'd made 126 jumps.

hint: Four lads from Liverpool landed in New York to screaming fans
funFact: Did you know? When the Beatles landed at JFK, 3,000 screaming fans met them. Police called it 'the most stressful duty' they'd ever pulled.

hint: A landmark law outlawed discrimination based on race and gender
funFact: Did you know? LBJ supposedly said after signing the Civil Rights Act: 'We have just lost the South for a generation.' He was almost right — it's been longer.

hint: A controversial activist was shot down while speaking in Harlem
funFact: Did you know? Malcolm X's autobiography was co-written with Alex Haley — who later wrote Roots. He interviewed Malcolm for 2 years before the assassination.

hint: A cosmonaut floated outside his capsule, the first spacewalk
funFact: Did you know? Leonov's spacewalk nearly killed him — his suit inflated so much he couldn't re-enter the capsule. He had to vent air secretly to squeeze back inside.

hint: A surprise offensive during a holiday shocked American forces
funFact: Did you know? The Tet Offensive was launched during a truce for Vietnamese New Year. It was a military defeat for the North — but a political victory they hadn't expected.

hint: A second Kennedy brother was shot during a campaign celebration
funFact: Did you know? RFK was shot in a hotel kitchen — moments after winning the California primary. Rosey Grier, an NFL linebacker, wrestled the gun away.

hint: Tanks rolled into Prague, ending a brief political spring
funFact: Did you know? When Soviet tanks rolled into Prague, some Czechs responded by removing street signs — so the invaders got lost. Civil disobedience, GPS-era style.

hint: Astronauts read Genesis while orbiting another world
funFact: Did you know? Apollo 8's crew read from Genesis on Christmas Eve — live from lunar orbit. It was the most-watched broadcast in history at the time.

hint: Half a million gathered on a farm for three days of peace and music
funFact: Did you know? Woodstock was supposed to be ticketed — but so many people showed up they just knocked down the fences. 400,000 attended. It rained nonstop.

hint: A young colonel seized power in Libya and held it for decades
funFact: Did you know? Gaddafi was 27 when he seized power. He then ruled for 42 years — at one point styling himself 'Brother Leader' and travelling with a Bedouin tent.

hint: A computer in California sent the first message to another computer
funFact: Did you know? The first ARPANET message was supposed to be 'LOGIN'. The system crashed after 'L' and 'O'. The internet's first word was 'LO'.

hint: Twenty million Americans rallied for the health of the planet
funFact: Did you know? The first Earth Day drew 20 million Americans — 10% of the population at the time. It helped push the Clean Air and Water Acts through Congress.

hint: National Guard opened fire on students protesting a war
funFact: Did you know? At Kent State, the National Guard was using live ammunition. Some students shot were 100+ metres away, just walking to class.

hint: A crippled spacecraft barely made it home from the Moon
funFact: Did you know? Apollo 13 used the lunar module as a lifeboat — it wasn't designed for it. The crew rigged a CO2 filter from duct tape, plastic bags, and a sock.

hint: A bungled break-in at a hotel would topple a president
funFact: Did you know? The Watergate burglars were caught because a security guard noticed a door's lock taped open. Frank Wills earned $80 a week. He later struggled to find work.

hint: A ceasefire ended direct US involvement in a Southeast Asian war
funFact: Did you know? The Paris Peace Accords took 5 years of talks. The hardest part? The shape of the negotiating table — it took 10 weeks to agree on that.

hint: Surprise attacks on a holy day launched a Middle Eastern war
funFact: Did you know? The Yom Kippur War caught Israel so off-guard that Golda Meir later said: 'The whole thing nearly fell apart because we believed our own intelligence.'

hint: Arab nations cut off oil, sending fuel prices sky-high
funFact: Did you know? OPEC's oil embargo quadrupled petrol prices. It's also why cars got smaller in the 70s — and why daylight saving became year-round in the US briefly.

hint: A revolution of flowers ended decades of dictatorship
funFact: Did you know? Portugal's Carnation Revolution was almost bloodless — soldiers stuck flowers in their rifle barrels instead of firing. A coup that smelled nice.

hint: A strongman was forced to flee Iraq as a new regime took power
event: Saddam Hussein takes power in Iraq
funFact: Did you know? Saddam Hussein had a doctorate in law and wrote romance novels. Yes, romance novels. They're real and they are, objectively, bad.

hint: Soviet troops crossed into Afghanistan, starting a decade of war
funFact: Did you know? The Soviet Afghan invasion lasted 10 years — and is often called the USSR's Vietnam. A generation of Soviet soldiers came home disillusioned.

hint: A border dispute sparked an eight-year war between neighbours
funFact: Did you know? The Iran-Iraq war lasted 8 years, killed a million+, and neither side gained any territory. It's been called 'the forgotten war'.

hint: A musical legend was shot outside his New York apartment
funFact: Did you know? John Lennon's killer had an autographed album from Lennon earlier that same evening. Lennon had paused, signed it, and moved on.

hint: A president was shot just 69 days into his term
funFact: Did you know? Reagan joked with doctors as he was wheeled into surgery: 'I hope you're all Republicans.' The lead surgeon replied: 'Today, Mr. President, we are all Republicans.'

hint: A royal wedding was watched by 750 million worldwide
funFact: Did you know? Diana's wedding dress had a 25-foot train — designed on the assumption the carriage was bigger than it actually was. They had to crumple the train to fit.

hint: An invasion of South Atlantic islands led to an unexpected war
funFact: Did you know? Argentina invaded the Falklands on April 2. The UK fleet sailed on April 5. Thatcher fought a war 8,000 miles away — and won it in 10 weeks.

hint: A dual concert raised millions for African famine relief
funFact: Did you know? Live Aid had 1.5 billion viewers — nearly 40% of humanity at the time. Queen's 20-minute set is still called the greatest live performance ever.

hint: A space station launched that would orbit for 15 years
funFact: Did you know? Mir was Soviet for 'peace' or 'world'. It was patched together in orbit over 10 years, and was so cramped that crews compared the smell to a wet basement.

hint: American jets struck a North African capital in retaliation
funFact: Did you know? The 1986 Libya bombing was ordered after a West Berlin disco bombing killed US soldiers. Gaddafi's compound was hit — his adopted daughter reportedly died.

hint: Tanks were halted by a lone man with a shopping bag
funFact: Did you know? We still don't know the identity of the Tank Man. Some say he was executed, others say he lived. All four tanks refused to run him over.

hint: A devastating earthquake struck during a World Series game
funFact: Did you know? The Loma Prieta quake hit during the World Series — millions were watching live when the broadcast cut out. Broadcasters literally felt the shaking.

hint: The first website went live, introducing the World Wide Web
funFact: Did you know? The first website is still online — it's a dense, blue-hyperlinked page by Tim Berners-Lee, explaining what the World Wide Web is. You can visit it today.

hint: A flag was lowered for the last time over the Kremlin
funFact: Did you know? The USSR ended with Gorbachev handing the nuclear briefcase to Yeltsin — then walking out. The red flag over the Kremlin came down that evening.

hint: Robert Watson-Watt demonstrated an early radio-based detection system.
funFact: Did you know? Radar was partly invented by accident — British scientists were asked to build a 'death ray' to bring down German planes. They couldn't, but invented radar instead.

hint: A presidential plane was shot down, triggering horror
funFact: Did you know? The Rwandan genocide killed an estimated 800,000 people in 100 days. UN peacekeepers were ordered NOT to intervene. It remains one of the great modern shames.

hint: A peace agreement ended decades of conflict in Northern Ireland
funFact: Did you know? The Good Friday Agreement was signed literally on Good Friday. Negotiators had been awake so long they lost track of days — the date was actually a coincidence.

hint: A president admitted an inappropriate relationship on TV
funFact: Did you know? Clinton's 'I did not have sexual relations with that woman' speech was rehearsed in a White House bathroom. Some reports say he practised in the mirror.

hint: NATO aircraft began bombing to stop ethnic cleansing
funFact: Did you know? NATO's Yugoslavia bombing was the first major combat use of stealth aircraft — one of which was shot down, surprising everyone.

hint: A school shooting shocked America and reignited gun debate
funFact: Did you know? Columbine changed US schools forever — but also inspired 'copycat' attacks for decades. Authorities now avoid publishing shooter names for this reason.

hint: A Russian leader resigned on the eve of a new millennium
funFact: Did you know? Yeltsin's resignation came in a televised speech where he asked Russians for forgiveness. His handpicked successor was a little-known Vladimir Putin.

hint: A space shuttle broke apart during re-entry over Texas
funFact: Did you know? Columbia disintegrated because a piece of foam hit the wing on launch — something NASA engineers had flagged as concerning, but were overruled on.

hint: A Russian president won a second term with a massive mandate
funFact: Did you know? Putin's 2004 re-election was essentially guaranteed — his main opposition candidate was a minor former senator nobody had heard of.

hint: Bombs on commuter trains killed 193 in a European capital
funFact: Did you know? The Madrid bombings came 3 days before an election. The ruling party blamed Basque separatists. The truth — Al-Qaeda — cost them the vote.

hint: A category 5 hurricane devastated the Gulf Coast
funFact: Did you know? Hurricane Katrina's levee failures flooded 80% of New Orleans. Some parts of the city remained underwater for weeks.

hint: Coordinated bombings struck a European capital's transport network
funFact: Did you know? The 7/7 bombers were all British. They bought their tickets like normal commuters. Londoners returned to work the same week — a very British response.

hint: A deposed dictator was executed by hanging
funFact: Did you know? Saddam was hanged from a gallows so short his body twisted as it fell — footage leaked online within hours. Executions used to be private; not anymore.

hint: A major bank collapsed, triggering a global financial crisis
funFact: Did you know? Lehman Brothers was founded in 1850. It survived two world wars and the Great Depression. It didn't survive 2008.

hint: A historic inauguration on the National Mall
funFact: Did you know? Obama's inauguration drew over 1.8 million people to the National Mall — the largest crowd ever gathered in Washington DC.

hint: The King of Pop's sudden death stunned the world
funFact: Did you know? Michael Jackson's funeral was watched by an estimated 2.5 billion people — more than watched the moon landing.

hint: A devastating earthquake struck a Caribbean nation
funFact: Did you know? The 2010 Haiti earthquake flattened 250,000 buildings in 35 seconds. The port was destroyed — so initial rescue ships couldn't even dock.

hint: A street vendor's protest sparked uprisings across a region
funFact: Did you know? The Arab Spring started when a Tunisian fruit seller, Mohamed Bouazizi, set himself on fire after police confiscated his cart. One act, multiple revolutions.

hint: An Egyptian president stepped down after 18 days of protest
funFact: Did you know? When Mubarak resigned, Tahrir Square erupted in cheers. The announcement came via the VP in a 30-second video. 30 years of rule, gone on camera.

hint: A decade-long manhunt ended in a compound in Pakistan
funFact: Did you know? The SEAL team that got bin Laden trained in a full-scale replica of his compound, built in Nevada. They memorised every door.

hint: Scientists announced discovering the particle that gives mass
funFact: Did you know? The Higgs boson was nicknamed the 'God Particle' — a name physicist Leon Lederman hated. He wanted to call it the 'Goddamn Particle' (it's so hard to find).

hint: White smoke signalled the first pope from the Americas
funFact: Did you know? Pope Francis is the first Jesuit pope, the first from the Americas, and the first to skip the papal Mercedes. He rides a Ford Focus.

hint: An extremist group seized a major city and declared a caliphate
funFact: Did you know? When ISIS took Mosul, its fighters captured $400 million in cash from Iraqi banks — instantly becoming the richest terrorist group in history.

hint: A passenger jet vanished without a trace over the open ocean
funFact: Did you know? MH370's disappearance sparked the largest search in aviation history — still ongoing in spirit. A few plane fragments have washed up in Madagascar and Mozambique.

hint: A nation voted to remain part of the United Kingdom
funFact: Did you know? The Scottish Referendum had a record 84.6% turnout — the highest for any UK election since universal suffrage.

hint: Gunmen attacked a satirical magazine's offices in Paris
funFact: Did you know? Charlie Hebdo had received threats for years. The attackers asked for staff by name. Survivors hid under desks; the publication was out the next week.

hint: Coordinated attacks struck a European capital on a Friday night
funFact: Did you know? The Paris attacks included coordinated assaults across 6 locations. One survivor owed her life to her mobile phone — it absorbed the bullet meant for her.

hint: A referendum narrowly voted to leave a continental union
funFact: Did you know? Brexit's 'Leave' campaign slogan — £350 million a week for the NHS — was quietly disavowed hours after winning. Campaign promises ended with the campaign.

hint: A businessman defeated expectations to win a presidential election
funFact: Did you know? Trump's 2016 win surprised even his own campaign team. Melania reportedly wasn't thrilled either. The polls had called it 85% for Clinton.

hint: A total solar eclipse swept across an entire continent
funFact: Did you know? The 2017 eclipse's path of totality crossed the US coast to coast — the first such eclipse since 1918. Hotels in tiny towns sold out for $500 a night.

hint: A gunman fired from a hotel window onto a music festival
funFact: Did you know? The Las Vegas shooter fired from the 32nd floor of the Mandalay Bay for just 10 minutes. The motive has never been officially determined.

hint: A rocket company launched a car into orbit around the Sun
funFact: Did you know? SpaceX launched Falcon Heavy carrying Elon Musk's own cherry-red Tesla Roadster — with a mannequin at the wheel. It's still out there, orbiting the sun.

hint: Two leaders met for the first time in a historic summit
funFact: Did you know? The Trump–Kim summit was the first meeting ever between a sitting US president and a North Korean leader. They met on an island for 13 hours.

hint: A teenager's school strike inspired a global climate movement
event: First global climate strike (Fridays for Future)
funFact: Did you know? Greta Thunberg's 'School Strike for Climate' started as one teenager sitting alone outside Swedish parliament. Within a year, 6 million were striking worldwide.

hint: Scientists captured the first image of a cosmic abyss
event: First image of a black hole released
funFact: Did you know? The first black hole photo took years of work by 200+ scientists using telescopes across 4 continents. The result? A doughnut-shaped blur — but a real one.

hint: Reports of a mysterious pneumonia cluster emerged from China
funFact: Did you know? COVID-19 was first publicly reported on December 31, 2019 — as 'pneumonia of unknown cause' in Wuhan. The world had 3 weeks of pretending it wouldn't spread.

hint: An island nation formally separated from a continental union
funFact: Did you know? Brexit Day, January 31 2020, was marked with a pro-Leave party in Parliament Square and a candlelit vigil in Edinburgh. Same country, two moods.

hint: A man's death in police custody ignited a global movement
funFact: Did you know? George Floyd was killed under a knee for 9 minutes 29 seconds. The teenager who filmed it, Darnella Frazier, later won a Pulitzer Prize.

hint: A mob stormed a legislative building in a shock to democracy
funFact: Did you know? The Capitol riot was live-streamed by many of its participants. Most were later identified by the FBI via their own phone footage.

hint: A militant group seized control after foreign forces withdrew
funFact: Did you know? The Taliban retook Kabul in 11 days — faster than anyone expected. US intelligence had predicted the Afghan government would last months.

hint: A massive ship blocked one of the world's busiest waterways
event: Ever Given blocks the Suez Canal
funFact: Did you know? The Ever Given was freed after 6 days — by tugboats and a backhoe that looked comically tiny next to it. It became a global meme within hours.

hint: The longest-reigning British monarch passed away at 96
funFact: Did you know? Elizabeth II was the first British monarch to reach a Platinum Jubilee (70 years). Her funeral drew ~4 billion viewers — the most-watched broadcast ever.

hint: A chatbot was released that sparked a new AI revolution
funFact: Did you know? ChatGPT hit 1 million users in 5 days — faster than any app in history. Facebook took 10 months for the same.

hint: Two inventors filed telephone patents on the very same day
event: Bell and Gray file telephone patents
funFact: Did you know? Elisha Gray filed his phone patent the SAME DAY as Bell — just hours later. Patent law's most famous photo finish.

hint: A practical electric light bulb finally glowed for hours
funFact: Did you know? Edison didn't invent the light bulb — he made the first commercially viable one. His key innovation was a carbonised cotton filament that lasted 1,200 hours.

hint: A wireless signal crossed the Atlantic for the first time
funFact: Did you know? Marconi's first transatlantic signal travelled 2,100 miles — though sceptics insisted it was just atmospheric noise. He was right, they were wrong.

hint: A phone call crossed the Atlantic Ocean for the first time
funFact: Did you know? The first transatlantic phone call cost $25 for 3 minutes in 1927 — about $400 today. You could buy a used car for that.

hint: A room-sized machine pioneered the age of electronic computing
funFact: Did you know? ENIAC weighed 30 tonnes, filled a room, and used 17,468 vacuum tubes. Your phone is about a million times faster — and doesn't need a cooling fan the size of a wardrobe.

hint: Six nations signed a treaty creating a common European market
event: Treaty of Rome (founding of the EEC)
funFact: Did you know? The Treaty of Rome created the EEC — what would become the EU. It was originally 6 countries. Now, minus the UK, it's 27.

hint: An astronaut orbited the Earth three times in a tiny capsule
funFact: Did you know? John Glenn, first American to orbit Earth, was also the oldest person ever in space — at age 77, on a 1998 Shuttle mission.

hint: An American astronaut floated outside his capsule for the first time
funFact: Did you know? Ed White didn't want to come back inside — he called it 'the saddest moment of my life' when ordered back in after 23 minutes outside.

hint: A second Moon mission launched just four months after the first
funFact: Did you know? Apollo 12 was struck by lightning TWICE during launch — 36 and 52 seconds after liftoff. The mission continued. 'NASA problem-solving' at its calmest.

hint: The first space station was launched into orbit
funFact: Did you know? Salyut 1 was the world's first space station — but its first crew, Soyuz 11, died on return when a valve failed. The only deaths in space to date.

hint: The first private film screening showed workers leaving a factory
funFact: Did you know? The Lumière brothers' first film private audience saw a train arriving at a station. The screen was tiny, but some attendees reportedly still gasped.

hint: A factory revolutionized manufacturing with a $5 daily wage
funFact: Did you know? Ford's $5 workday doubled wages overnight. Critics called him reckless. Turnover plummeted — and his workers could now afford his cars.

hint: A giant ape climbed a skyscraper on the silver screen
event: King Kong premieres in New York
funFact: Did you know? King Kong was filmed with a 45cm model and stop-motion animation. The Empire State Building scene took weeks to shoot, frame by frame.

hint: A spacecraft made the first soft landing on another world
funFact: Did you know? Surveyor 1 landed successfully despite being a completely automated mission — 7 months before the first manned Moon landing rehearsal.

hint: A surgeon transplanted a human heart for the very first time
funFact: Did you know? The first heart transplant patient lived 18 days. The second lived 19 months. Christiaan Barnard became such a celebrity he dated Gina Lollobrigida.

hint: A space opera debuted that would become a cultural empire
funFact: Did you know? Star Wars was famously rejected by every studio except Fox. George Lucas took a $500k pay cut in exchange for merchandising rights. He retired a billionaire.

hint: The first baby conceived outside the body was born
event: Birth of Louise Brown (first IVF baby)
funFact: Did you know? Louise Brown was announced as the first IVF baby — but she was born the day before her birth announcement, to protect her family from the press. She's now a mum herself.

hint: A stadium crush killed 97 football fans at a semi-final
funFact: Did you know? Hillsborough was finally ruled unlawful killing in 2016 — 27 years after 97 football fans were crushed. Families fought that long for the truth.

hint: Troops cleared a square after weeks of pro-democracy protest
funFact: Did you know? The Tiananmen Square massacre remains officially denied in China — search engines there censor the date. The iconic Tank Man photo is banned.

hint: A predawn earthquake devastated a California valley
funFact: Did you know? The Northridge quake killed 57 and caused $50 billion in damage — the costliest US quake ever. Freeways collapsed; one bridge fell twice.

hint: Russian forces entered a breakaway republic, starting a war
funFact: Did you know? The First Chechen War humiliated Russia's military — 80,000+ troops struggled for 2 years against a much smaller Chechen force.

hint: A nerve gas attack struck a Tokyo subway during rush hour
funFact: Did you know? The Tokyo sarin attackers released bags on subway trains using sharpened umbrellas. 13 died; 6,000 were injured. Tokyo's subway has since been on high alert.

hint: A UN safe area fell, leading to Europe's worst post-WWII massacre
funFact: Did you know? Srebrenica was supposed to be a 'UN safe area'. 8,000+ Bosnian Muslims were killed anyway. A subsequent tribunal classified it as genocide.

hint: A rover landed on Mars and sent back stunning photos
funFact: Did you know? Spirit rover was designed for 90 Martian days. It worked for over 6 years. The Mars surface is unforgiving on everything except NASA engineers.

hint: Parisians captured a medieval fortress, igniting a revolution.
funFact: Did you know? The Bastille held only 7 prisoners when stormed — 4 forgers, 2 'lunatics', and 1 'libertine'. Symbolism beat strategy that day.

hint: A probe made the first-ever landing on a comet's surface
event: Philae lander touches down on comet 67P
funFact: Did you know? Philae landed on comet 67P but bounced twice on landing — into shadow. Its solar panels couldn't charge. Still — humanity had landed on a comet.

hint: A rover the size of a car landed on Mars using a sky crane
funFact: Did you know? Curiosity's landing used a 'sky crane' — lowering the rover by cables from a rocket-powered platform. NASA called the landing '7 minutes of terror'.

hint: The first modern athletic games opened in their ancient homeland
funFact: Did you know? The 1896 Olympics only had 14 nations. One American, James Connolly, became the first modern Olympic champion by winning the triple jump.

hint: A famous aviator vanished over the Pacific attempting a world flight
funFact: Did you know? Earhart was heading for Howland Island — a spot 2km wide in the Pacific. Her disappearance is still one of aviation's greatest mysteries.

hint: A baseball player broke the colour barrier in a major league
funFact: Did you know? Jackie Robinson broke baseball's colour barrier — and got death threats, slurs, even beanballs. His manager told him: 'I want a ballplayer who has the guts not to fight back.'

hint: A motorist's beating by police was caught on video
funFact: Did you know? The King beating video was filmed by a plumber with a new camcorder. The tape was nearly sold for $500 — but a local TV station bought it instead.

hint: A federal agency was created to investigate crimes across states
funFact: Did you know? The FBI originally had just 34 agents. It was called the Bureau of Investigation — only became 'Federal' in 1935. J. Edgar Hoover joined as a clerk.

hint: US soldiers killed hundreds of unarmed villagers in Vietnam
funFact: Did you know? My Lai was uncovered by a whistleblower — a helicopter pilot who landed between US soldiers and Vietnamese civilians to stop the killings.

hint: Two leaders met secretly on warships to sign a charter of principles
funFact: Did you know? The Atlantic Charter was drafted without the US even being at war. Roosevelt and Churchill sketched a post-war order 4 months before Pearl Harbor.

hint: An international conference established a prime meridian
funFact: Did you know? The Greenwich Meridian was chosen partly because most maps already used it. France voted 'no' and clung to Paris time for another 27 years.

hint: Two rival space programs linked up in orbit for the first time
funFact: Did you know? The Apollo-Soyuz handshake happened 140 miles above Earth. The meal afterwards included borscht in squeezy tubes labelled 'vodka' as a joke.

hint: Soldiers in Egypt found a stone that would unlock ancient writing
funFact: Did you know? The Rosetta Stone was found by French soldiers digging a fort. The British seized it after beating Napoleon. It's been in the British Museum since 1802.

hint: A spacecraft looked back and captured Earth as a pale blue dot
funFact: Did you know? Voyager 1's 'Pale Blue Dot' photo was taken from 3.7 billion miles. Earth is one pixel wide. Carl Sagan called it 'a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam'.

hint: A rover named for a trailblazer rolled across Martian soil
funFact: Did you know? Pathfinder's Sojourner rover was about the size of a microwave oven. It was the first successful Mars rover and ran 12 times its planned lifespan.

hint: The first module of a great orbital outpost was launched
funFact: Did you know? ISS construction took 12 years and 42 launches. Parts were built in 5 countries. Somehow they all fit together in orbit. Engineers deserve a gold medal.

hint: A spacecraft entered orbit around a ringed planet for the first time
funFact: Did you know? Cassini orbited Saturn for 13 years — sending back so much data that scientists are still analysing it years after the mission ended.

hint: A probe parachuted onto the surface of a distant moon
funFact: Did you know? Huygens is the only probe to land on a moon of another planet. It recorded the sounds of Titan's wind — the first alien audio ever heard by humans.

hint: Astronomers demoted a beloved ninth planet to dwarf status
funFact: Did you know? Pluto was demoted partly because we kept finding bigger objects beyond it. If it's still a planet, we'd have to admit about 200 more.

hint: Scientists announced detecting ripples in spacetime itself
funFact: Did you know? LIGO detected ripples in spacetime from two black holes colliding — an event that happened 1.3 billion years ago. The wave had a long commute.

hint: A private company launched astronauts to orbit for the first time
event: SpaceX Crew Dragon first crewed launch
funFact: Did you know? Crew Dragon was the first commercial spacecraft to carry people to orbit. The touchscreen controls were a radical departure from decades of button-covered cockpits.

hint: A tiny helicopter achieved powered flight on another planet
funFact: Did you know? Ingenuity was originally planned for 5 flights. It eventually completed 72 before breaking a rotor. It was the first powered flight on another planet.

hint: A space telescope launched to peer into the dawn of the cosmos
funFact: Did you know? JWST was the most expensive telescope ever built — $10 billion — and launched perfectly. Mission planners cried at the first image.

hint: A subterranean railway opened beneath the streets of London
funFact: Did you know? The London Underground's 1863 opening ran on steam engines — passengers emerged black with soot. They called it 'ventilation was an optional extra'.

hint: A nation crowned its first consul as emperor of the French
funFact: Did you know? Napoleon's Emperor proclamation was technically approved by a plebiscite with a 99% yes vote. Those who voted no may have preferred to stay anonymous.

hint: A divided nation was reunited after 45 years apart
funFact: Did you know? German reunification happened 11 months after the Berlin Wall fell. Chancellor Kohl had pushed hard — some European leaders, Thatcher included, were uneasy.

hint: A Renaissance master breathed his last in the arms of a king
funFact: Did you know? Leonardo da Vinci died in France — reportedly in the arms of King Francis I. He left behind 13,000 pages of notes, most of which nobody has read fully.

hint: Viking raiders sacked a holy island off the English coast
funFact: Did you know? The Lindisfarne raid started the Viking Age. Monks described it as 'unlooked for'. The Vikings saw coastal monasteries as poorly defended gold stores.

hint: A Spanish explorer first sighted the vast Pacific Ocean
funFact: Did you know? Balboa crossed Panama and saw the Pacific from a hilltop. He waded in waist-deep, sword raised, claiming the entire ocean for Spain. Humble guy.

hint: A peaceful march to the sea challenged an empire's salt tax
funFact: Did you know? Gandhi's Salt March was 240 miles, took 24 days, and ended with him scooping up salt in defiance of British tax law. It triggered 80,000 arrests.

hint: A scientist was forced to deny the Earth moves around the Sun
funFact: Did you know? Galileo reportedly muttered 'and yet it moves' after being forced to renounce heliocentrism. Almost certainly apocryphal. Still a great line.

hint: A teenager's diary was silenced when soldiers found their hiding place
funFact: Did you know? Anne Frank's family was betrayed after 2 years in hiding. Her diary was saved by Miep Gies — who kept it unread, so it could be returned if Anne came back.

hint: A secret meeting planned a horrifying 'final solution'
funFact: Did you know? The Wannsee Conference was 90 minutes long. Fifteen officials planned the 'Final Solution'. Minutes survived — one attendee kept a copy.

hint: Soviet soldiers liberated a death camp, revealing the horror within
funFact: Did you know? When Soviet troops liberated Auschwitz, they found 7,000 survivors, 370,000 men's suits, and 8 tonnes of human hair. The Nazis had been shipping everything back as product.

hint: A female spy was executed by a French firing squad at dawn
funFact: Did you know? Mata Hari was an exotic dancer who became a double agent in WWI — poorly. French intelligence shot her for spying. Her information was reportedly useless.

hint: A president asked Congress to make the world safe for democracy
funFact: Did you know? Wilson campaigned in 1916 on the slogan 'He kept us out of war.' A year later, America joined WWI anyway. Political promises, 1917 edition.

hint: A mushroom cloud rose over a New Mexico desert at dawn
funFact: Did you know? The Trinity nuclear test lit up the desert so brightly that a blind girl 120 miles away 'saw' the flash. Oppenheimer quoted the Bhagavad Gita.

hint: A hurricane devastated the Gulf Coast, killing over 250
funFact: Did you know? Hurricane Camille was a Category 5 — winds so strong they blew grass out of the ground. In some areas, anemometers broke before recording the peak.

hint: The WHO declared a deadly disease had been eradicated worldwide
funFact: Did you know? Smallpox is the only human disease ever eradicated. The WHO confirmed it in 1980. Some labs still keep samples — locked in freezers in Russia and the US.

hint: A spacecraft became the first to cross beyond Neptune's orbit
funFact: Did you know? Pioneer 10 is now over 13 billion miles from Earth. Its last faint signal was in 2003. It's still out there, drifting toward the star Aldebaran.

hint: A spacecraft plunged into a gas giant after 20 years of exploration
funFact: Did you know? Cassini's Grand Finale involved plunging INTO Saturn — so it couldn't contaminate moons that might harbour life. Mission control played a dirge in its honour.

hint: A probe achieved the first landing on the far side of another world
event: Chang'e 4 lands on far side of Moon
funFact: Did you know? Chang'e 4 was the first probe to land on the Moon's far side — the side we never see from Earth. China also deployed the first cotton seeds on the Moon.

hint: A rover landed in a crater lake bed seeking signs of ancient life
funFact: Did you know? Perseverance carried Ingenuity, a mini-helicopter, as hitchhiker — strapped to its belly. It's also filled with samples for a future Mars-return mission.

hint: The architect of the Terror lost his own head to the blade
funFact: Did you know? Robespierre was executed the day after he tried to shoot himself — and missed, shattering his jaw. The Jacobin leader's own Terror caught up with him.

hint: A teenage Austrian princess married the future king of France
event: Marriage of Marie Antoinette and Louis XVI
funFact: Did you know? Marie Antoinette was 14, Louis 15 when they married. She'd been sent from Austria with 57 carriages and 376 horses. Diplomatic weddings were never quiet.

hint: Women marching for bread sparked a revolution that toppled a tsar
funFact: Did you know? The 1917 February Revolution started with women textile workers striking for bread. The 'February Revolution' was actually in March — thanks to Russia's old Julian calendar.

hint: A royal family was executed in a basement in the Urals
funFact: Did you know? The Romanov family was shot in a basement by Bolsheviks. Bullets reportedly bounced off the daughters — they'd sewn diamonds into their corsets.

hint: A new nation separated from its larger southern neighbour
funFact: Did you know? Panama's independence was engineered by the US — which wanted to build a canal Colombia had refused. 'Nation-building', early 20th-century edition.

hint: A great unsinkable ship departed on its maiden voyage
event: RMS Titanic sets sail from Southampton
funFact: Did you know? Titanic set sail from Southampton carrying 2,224 passengers. Its lifeboats held only 1,178. Even if every boat had been full, 1,046 would have had no seat.

hint: A devastating explosion flattened a harbour city in Canada
funFact: Did you know? The Halifax explosion was the largest man-made blast before the atomic bomb. A French munitions ship collided with a Norwegian ship in Halifax Harbour.

hint: Two friends started building computers in a California garage
funFact: Did you know? Apple Computer was founded in a California garage by 3 people: Steve Jobs (21), Steve Wozniak (25), and Ron Wayne — who sold his 10% share for $800. It would later be worth billions.

hint: A world leader challenged his rival to tear down a wall
funFact: Did you know? Reagan's 'Tear Down This Wall' speech was almost cut from the final draft. Aides thought it too provocative. He kept it in. 2 years later, the wall fell.

hint: An allied counter-offensive began that would end the Great War
funFact: Did you know? The Second Marne battle used new French tactics — tanks and air support together. It's considered the turning point where WWI started swinging Allied.

hint: A new British PM promised nothing but blood, toil, tears, and sweat
funFact: Did you know? Churchill became PM the same day Germany invaded France. He said he felt as if he was 'walking with destiny'. Destiny had not been gentle lately.

hint: A patent was granted that would connect the world by voice
funFact: Did you know? Bell's telephone patent, US 174,465, is often called 'the most valuable patent ever issued'. It was approved weeks before a rival filing could be reviewed.

hint: An African nation gained independence, starting a wave across the continent
funFact: Did you know? The Belgian Congo's independence came with a speech by new PM Lumumba that was so critical of Belgium that the King nearly walked out.

hint: A manifesto warned of nuclear weapons' threat to civilization
funFact: Did you know? Einstein and Russell wrote their anti-nuclear manifesto together. Einstein signed it just days before he died — making it one of his final acts.

hint: A revolution ended thousands of years of imperial rule
funFact: Did you know? The Wuchang Uprising was partly triggered by an accidental bomb explosion that exposed revolutionary plans. Clumsiness toppled a 2,000-year-old empire.

hint: A communist leader proclaimed a new people's republic
event: Founding of the People's Republic of China
funFact: Did you know? When Mao proclaimed the PRC, he stood atop Tiananmen Gate and reportedly fumbled the announcement microphone. Not the smoothest foundational moment.

hint: Two rival dictators shocked the world with a non-aggression pact
funFact: Did you know? The Nazi-Soviet pact shocked the world — two ideological enemies becoming allies. It lasted 22 months before Hitler invaded anyway.

hint: A couple was executed for allegedly passing atomic secrets
funFact: Did you know? The Rosenbergs were the only US civilians ever executed for espionage. Their sons have spent decades arguing for their innocence. Partial declassification later showed Julius likely spied; Ethel less so.

hint: A small garrison fell after a 13-day siege in Texas
funFact: Did you know? Davy Crockett died at the Alamo — possibly captured and executed rather than killed in the battle. The siege lasted 13 days.

hint: Twin brothers founded a city on seven hills
funFact: Did you know? Romulus is said to have killed his brother Remus in a dispute over where to build the city. The date is legendary — nothing from 753 BC actually survives.

hint: A gas was isolated that would prove essential for breathing
funFact: Did you know? Priestley discovered oxygen but called it 'dephlogisticated air'. The name didn't catch on. Lavoisier later renamed it, and took most of the credit.

hint: A French civil code was enacted that reshaped European law
funFact: Did you know? The Napoleonic Code still underpins French civil law today — and influenced the legal systems of over 70 countries. Not bad for one man's project.

hint: A tax on earnings was introduced for the first time in Britain
event: First income tax introduced in Britain
funFact: Did you know? Britain's first income tax was 10% — to fund wars against Napoleon. It was supposed to be temporary. It is still, somehow, not temporary.

hint: Portuguese navigators landed on the coast of South America
funFact: Did you know? The Portuguese landed in Brazil 8 years after Columbus reached America. They claimed it under a papal treaty that had drawn a literal line across the map.

hint: A radio broadcast about an alien invasion caused mass panic
event: War of the Worlds radio broadcast
funFact: Did you know? Orson Welles's 'War of the Worlds' caused some listeners to panic — but historians now think the scale of public hysteria was exaggerated by newspapers hostile to radio.

hint: A global health organisation was formally established
funFact: Did you know? The WHO was founded on April 7 — now celebrated yearly as World Health Day. Its first big project was coordinating the smallpox eradication campaign.

hint: Three prisoners escaped from an island fortress through a vent
funFact: Did you know? Three men escaped Alcatraz using raincoats stitched into a raft and dummy heads made of soap and real hair. Nobody knows if they survived — the FBI closed the case in 2012.

hint: A legendary guitarist died at 27 in London
funFact: Did you know? Hendrix died aged 27 — joining the '27 Club' that would soon include Joplin and Morrison. He'd been playing guitar left-handed on upside-down right-handed strings.

hint: A blues-rock singer passed away at 27 in Los Angeles
funFact: Did you know? Janis Joplin died just 16 days after Hendrix. Both from overdoses. Within 9 months, Jim Morrison would make it 3.

hint: A legendary rock singer died at 27 in Paris
funFact: Did you know? Jim Morrison was found dead in a Paris bathtub. No autopsy was performed. Conspiracy theories still thrive — his grave in Père Lachaise is one of Paris's most visited.

hint: A baseball legend broke the all-time home run record
event: Hank Aaron breaks home run record
funFact: Did you know? Hank Aaron got so much hate mail and so many death threats approaching Babe Ruth's record that the FBI got involved. He broke the record anyway.

hint: A test pilot broke the sound barrier in a rocket plane
event: Chuck Yeager breaks the sound barrier
funFact: Did you know? Yeager broke the sound barrier with two cracked ribs — he'd fallen off a horse 2 days earlier. He used the end of a broomstick to close the cockpit door one-handed.

hint: A cavalry commander's last stand against Lakota warriors
funFact: Did you know? Custer was reportedly warned repeatedly that he was outnumbered. He divided his forces anyway. 268 died. The Lakota and Cheyenne won — briefly.

hint: Coalition forces began a campaign in a mountainous nation
funFact: Did you know? The US invasion of Afghanistan was the longest war in American history — 20 years. It ended with a chaotic withdrawal and the Taliban back in power.

hint: A close asteroid flyby will be visible to the naked eye
funFact: Did you know? Asteroid Apophis will pass closer to Earth than some satellites — but won't hit. Astronomers will have a front-row seat. Telescope tickets, please.

hint: A living fossil fish was caught off the coast of South Africa
funFact: Did you know? The coelacanth was thought extinct for 65 million years — until a South African fisherman netted one in 1938. It's now called a 'living fossil'.

hint: A satellite was launched that enabled live transatlantic TV
funFact: Did you know? Telstar 1 was the first satellite to relay live TV, phone, and data. Its broadcasts had to be perfectly timed — the satellite only overhead for 20 minutes at a time.

hint: A group of pilgrims departed England for the New World
funFact: Did you know? The Mayflower was built as a wine trader, not a passenger ship. 102 pilgrims squeezed into a vessel 30 metres long. Two died at sea. One was born on board.

hint: Pilgrims signed a compact before stepping ashore
funFact: Did you know? The Mayflower Compact was one of the first self-governance documents in the New World. It was written because they'd landed off-course and lacked a royal charter.

hint: A friar's bonfire destroyed art and luxury goods in Florence
funFact: Did you know? Savonarola's Bonfire of the Vanities burned books, cosmetics, and even paintings. A year later, Florentines burned him — on the same spot. Symmetry.

hint: A nurse who would transform battlefield care was born
funFact: Did you know? Nightingale invented the pie chart to show mortality causes in the Crimea. She saved lives — and also low-key founded modern data visualisation.

hint: A camera was marketed with the slogan 'You press the button'
funFact: Did you know? Kodak's slogan was 'You press the button, we do the rest' — meaning you literally mailed your camera to Kodak, who developed it and sent back prints.

hint: Marines landed on a Pacific island to begin a gruelling campaign
funFact: Did you know? Guadalcanal was the Pacific War's Stalingrad — a 6-month slog that cost both sides dearly. It was the first major Allied offensive against Japan.

hint: A philosopher was burned at the stake for heretical ideas
funFact: Did you know? Giordano Bruno was burned for suggesting infinite worlds and stars as distant suns. He got most of his physics right — and died for it.

hint: A journalist famously found a missing explorer in Africa
funFact: Did you know? Stanley's 'Dr. Livingstone, I presume?' was probably never said — Livingstone's own journals don't mention it, and Stanley tore out the page. Journalism's oldest famous quote may be fiction.

hint: A golden bridge opened, connecting a city to a northern headland
funFact: Did you know? The Golden Gate Bridge's iconic 'international orange' was chosen for visibility in fog. The US Navy wanted it painted in yellow and black stripes.

hint: A German chemist trademarked a pain-relieving compound
funFact: Did you know? Aspirin was originally stronger than heroin — both trademarks Bayer owned. Heroin was sold as a cough medicine. The 1900s were wild.

hint: Federal agents ambushed America's most wanted outside a cinema
funFact: Did you know? Dillinger had plastic surgery to disguise himself — and tried to burn off his fingerprints with acid. The FBI found him anyway. A woman in red tipped them off.

hint: A pharmacist in Atlanta invented a drink that would conquer the world
funFact: Did you know? Coca-Cola originally contained cocaine. It was removed in 1903 — replaced by caffeine from kola nuts (hence the name). Kinda sounds safer.

hint: A fashion doll debuted that would become a cultural icon
funFact: Did you know? Barbie's creator based her on a German doll marketed to men. She made Barbie for American girls — and named her after her own daughter.

hint: A 24-hour news channel launched, changing media forever
funFact: Did you know? CNN was founded as a 24-hour news channel when nobody believed 24-hour news could work. Ted Turner was told 'no one watches TV all day'. Turner persevered.

hint: Soldiers strung barbed wire across a city's heart at midnight
funFact: Did you know? The Berlin Wall started as barbed wire and sandbags — it took weeks to build the famous concrete version. Thousands escaped in the interim.

hint: An engineer made the first call from a handheld mobile phone
funFact: Did you know? The first mobile phone call was made by a Motorola engineer — to his rival at Bell Labs, just to gloat. The phone weighed over a kilogram.

hint: A president pledged to put a man on the Moon before the decade's end
event: JFK's 'We choose to go to the Moon' speech
funFact: Did you know? Kennedy's 'we choose to go to the Moon' speech was made at a stadium in Texas heat. Crowds fanned themselves as he promised the Moon within 8 years.

hint: A tech company released the first commercial microprocessor
funFact: Did you know? The Intel 4004 chip had 2,300 transistors. Today's chips have billions. You could fit roughly 10 million Intel 4004s on a single modern die.

hint: A new music television channel played its first video
funFact: Did you know? MTV launched with the Buggles' 'Video Killed the Radio Star'. A prophecy and a theme song in one. The decade of music videos was born.

hint: A solar-powered rover left Earth heading to Mars
funFact: Did you know? Spirit's twin, Opportunity, was launched 4 weeks later. Both were designed for 3 months. Opportunity lasted 15 years — until a dust storm finally stopped it.

hint: A notorious island prison in a bay was officially closed
funFact: Did you know? Alcatraz closed because it cost 3x as much to run as any other federal prison — everything had to be shipped in. Even water. Crime pays, apparently. Prisons don't.

hint: A chess computer beat a world champion for the first time
funFact: Did you know? Deep Blue won one game against Kasparov in 1996 but lost the match. The 1997 rematch — when Deep Blue won — is often called chess's human-vs-machine turning point.

hint: A computer finally defeated the world chess champion in a match
funFact: Did you know? After losing to Deep Blue, Kasparov accused IBM of cheating by having humans secretly intervene. IBM refused a rematch and dismantled the machine.

hint: A microblogging platform launched with 140-character messages
funFact: Did you know? Twitter's first tweet was 'just setting up my twttr' — by co-founder Jack Dorsey. It later sold as an NFT for $2.9 million. The buyer regretted it.

hint: A tech CEO unveiled a device that would change everything
funFact: Did you know? Steve Jobs introduced the iPhone with the line 'An iPod, a phone, and an internet communicator.' The crowd clapped. Then realised — wait, that's one device.

hint: The US Supreme Court upheld a landmark healthcare law
event: Affordable Care Act upheld by Supreme Court
funFact: Did you know? Chief Justice Roberts sided with the liberal wing in 2012 to save the ACA — stunning conservatives. The deciding vote came down to how they legally classified the individual mandate.

hint: Marriage equality was made the law of the land
event: US Supreme Court legalises same-sex marriage
funFact: Did you know? Obergefell v. Hodges made same-sex marriage legal nationwide. The lead plaintiff, Jim Obergefell, was fighting to be named his late husband's spouse on a death certificate.

hint: Britain detonated its first nuclear weapon in an Australian bay
funFact: Did you know? Britain's first nuclear test was at the Monte Bello Islands, off Australia — on a ship that was vaporised. It was the UK's ticket into the nuclear club.

hint: A reusable spacecraft launched into orbit for the very first time
funFact: Did you know? Columbia was the first Space Shuttle to reach orbit. Its launch was delayed 2 years. It would fly 28 missions before disintegrating on re-entry in 2003.

hint: A revolutionary commune briefly governed a European capital
funFact: Did you know? The Paris Commune lasted just 2 months. Its brief rule included separation of church and state, women's rights proposals, and workers' cooperatives — radical for 1871.

hint: A tech visionary and Apple co-founder passed away
funFact: Did you know? Steve Jobs's final reported words were 'Oh wow. Oh wow. Oh wow.' His sister was at his side. The man who built Apple made one last apt pitch.

hint: A band from Liverpool appeared on American TV to 73 million viewers
event: Beatles perform on The Ed Sullivan Show
funFact: Did you know? The Beatles' Ed Sullivan debut drew 73 million viewers — about 40% of America. Crime rates reportedly dropped during the broadcast.

hint: An amendment granted women the right to vote in America
funFact: Did you know? The 19th Amendment gave American women the vote — 72 years after the Seneca Falls Convention first demanded it. Progress is sometimes slow, but it arrives.

hint: An assassination attempt was made on a pope in St. Peter's Square
event: Pope John Paul II assassination attempt
funFact: Did you know? Pope John Paul II survived 4 bullets at close range. He later met his would-be assassin in prison and reportedly forgave him. The bullet is now in a Marian shrine.

hint: A legendary physicist and pacifist died in New Jersey
funFact: Did you know? Einstein's brain was removed (without permission) during his autopsy, sliced into 240 pieces, and stored in jars. Parts went on a road trip. Parts may still be missing.

hint: A war criminal went on trial in Israel after being captured in Argentina
funFact: Did you know? Eichmann's trial was one of the first broadcast on TV globally. He argued he was 'just following orders'. The tribunal hanged him; his ashes were scattered at sea.

hint: A captivating open-world fantasy RPG was released to massive acclaim
event: The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim released
funFact: Did you know? Skyrim launched on 11/11/11 — and now has more mods than any other game. It's been re-released 8 times. You literally cannot escape Skyrim.

hint: An oil rig exploded in the Gulf of Mexico, causing a massive spill
funFact: Did you know? Deepwater Horizon spilled oil for 87 days straight — 4.9 million barrels. It was the largest marine oil spill in history. Satellites tracked it from space.

hint: The First Fleet arrived, marking the beginning of European settlement
funFact: Did you know? The First Fleet carried 11 ships, ~1,400 people, and almost no farmers. Starvation nearly wiped the colony out in its first 2 years.

hint: Thirty-three miners were rescued after 69 days underground
funFact: Did you know? The 33 Chilean miners spent 69 days underground — the longest survival in a mine. They were hoisted out one by one in a capsule called Phoenix.

hint: The King of Rock and Roll was found dead at his Memphis estate
funFact: Did you know? Elvis's funeral had 80,000 fans gather outside Graceland. He'd made $4.9 million in his final year alive — plus countless millions posthumously.

hint: The first telegraph message asked 'What hath God wrought?'
funFact: Did you know? Morse's first message was 'What hath God wrought' — a Bible quote. Picked by the daughter of a colleague. The telegraph age officially began.

hint: German bombers began sustained night attacks on a capital city
funFact: Did you know? The Blitz lasted 57 consecutive nights. Londoners slept in Underground stations for months. One newspaper headline read 'Britain can take it' — and, somehow, did.

hint: Scientists announced they had cloned a mammal from an adult cell
funFact: Did you know? Dolly the sheep was named after Dolly Parton — because she was cloned from a mammary gland cell. Scientists have always had a sense of humour.

hint: German troops marched into a capital city left undefended
event: Fall of Paris to Nazi Germany
funFact: Did you know? When Paris fell, most Parisians just … left. Over 2 million fled before the Nazis arrived. The occupiers marched into a half-empty city.

hint: Three small ships departed Spain seeking a westward route to Asia
funFact: Did you know? Columbus set out with 3 ships and about 90 men — and thought he'd reached India. He died insisting he had. The Americas are named for someone else entirely.

hint: A partial nuclear meltdown alarmed the eastern United States
funFact: Did you know? Three Mile Island was America's worst nuclear accident — though no one died. It still set back US nuclear power by decades. The reactor is still there, sealed.

hint: The first national park in the world was established
funFact: Did you know? Yellowstone was the world's first national park. Grant signed it into law partly because no one wanted it for farming — it was 'useless' land. Now it's priceless.

hint: A patent was granted for the first practical writing machine
funFact: Did you know? Typewriters originally had keys in alphabetical order. QWERTY was designed to SLOW typists down, because adjacent keys kept jamming on the fastest machines.
